interest:
I study JWST observations of high-redshift galaxies and AGN, especially
little red dots (LRDs), compact red sources, dust-reddened or broad-line AGN,
early black-hole growth, and galaxy/AGN co-evolution at cosmic dawn.

Prioritize papers about:
1. JWST/NIRCam/NIRSpec/MIRI observations of high-redshift galaxies and AGN
2. little red dots, compact red galaxies, obscured AGN, broad-line AGN, and
   high-redshift black hole candidates
3. SED fitting, spectroscopy, emission lines, photometric redshifts, stellar
   masses, dust attenuation, AGN contamination, and source classification
4. high-redshift galaxy formation, reionization-era galaxies, early SMBH
   growth, and galaxy/AGN co-evolution
5. survey papers from CEERS, JADES, UNCOVER, COSMOS-Web, PRIMER, GLASS,
   RUBIES, and similar JWST deep fields

Also keep papers about AI, machine learning, large language models (LLMs),
large multimodal models (LMMs), foundation models, anomaly detection,
automated classification, spectral/photometric inference, or research agents
when they are applied to astronomy, astrophysics, JWST data, galaxy surveys,
AGN selection, or literature/data analysis.

Deprioritize unrelated stellar, solar-system, local-universe, gravitational
wave, or purely theoretical papers unless they directly inform high-redshift
galaxies, AGN, JWST analysis, or AI-for-astronomy workflows.

papers.title: BlackTHUNDER Reveals a Massive Filament around a Compact AGN at $z\simeq5.23$
papers.authors: Giulia Tozzi , Hannah Übler , Eleonora Parlanti , Roberto Maiolino , Claudia Pulsoni , Rachel Somerville , Mirko Curti , Giovanni Mazzolari , Capucine Barfety , Elena Bertola , Andrew J. Bunker , Stefano Carniani , Giovanni Cresci , Richard Davies , Francesco D'Eugenio , Frank Eisenhauer , Natascha M. Förster Schreiber , Reinhard Genzel , Lucy R. Ivey , Ignas Juodžbalis , Dieter Lutz , Cosimo Marconcini , Thorsten Naab , Meghana Pannikkote , Stavros Pastras , Michele Perna , Letizia Scaloni , Raffaella Schneider , Linda J. Tacconi , Giacomo Venturi
papers.abstract: Despite the growing number of compact active galactic nuclei (AGN) at $z>4$ discovered by JWST, their formation and evolution remain poorly understood. This paper investigates the large-scale environment of GN-77652, a compact AGN at $z=5.229$ observed as part of the JWST NIRSpec IFU Large Program BlackTHUNDER and complemented by deep multi-band NIRCam imaging. GN-77652 lies in close proximity to a 12 kpc-long filament composed of multiple sources at $z\simeq5.23$, spanning a remarkable range in stellar masses ($M_{\star}=0.7-13 \times 10^8$ ${M_\odot}$), gas phase metallicities (12$+$log(O/H) $=$ 7.6-8.5) and star formation rates (SFR $=0.4-6$ ${M_\odot}$ yr$^{-1}$). The [OIII]$\lambda$5007 kinematics reveals a smooth large-scale velocity gradient centred on the central, massive ($M_{\star}\simeq1.1\times10^9$ ${M_\odot}$) and metal rich ($Z\sim0.6$ $Z_{\odot}$) system of the group. In this source, only 2.4 kpc (projected) from GN-77652, [OIII]$\lambda$4363 line diagnostics provide possible evidence for a second AGN. GN-77652 exhibits a shallow ($-30$ to $+20$ km s$^{-1}$) velocity gradient that is consistent with disk rotation according to dynamical modelling. The Lyman-Werner radiation field produced by the filament is too weak for the black hole (BH) in GN-77652 to have formed recently via direct collapse. However, the required conditions may have existed at earlier epochs, or alternative scenarios (e.g. a recoiling BH ejected from the filament) could also be plausible. The whole system is expected to coalesce in $150-440$ Myr, also motivating an exploration of its future evolution through toy-model extrapolations and numerical simulations. Our analysis suggests that the compact AGN appearance of GN-77652 represents a transient evolutionary phase, consistent with the apparent decline with redshift in number density of compact AGN identified with JWST.
papers.Reasons for match: Directly studies a compact AGN at z~5.23 with JWST NIRSpec IFU and NIRCam, including environment, kinematics, and BH formation scenarios.
papers.Short digest: The paper asks how compact AGN at z>4 form and evolve, using JWST observations of GN-77652. It finds a massive filament around the AGN with a second possible AGN, and suggests the compact AGN phase is transient. This is highly relevant to my work on JWST observations of high-redshift AGN, LRDs, and early BH growth.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check the [OIII] kinematics and velocity gradient evidence for disk rotation.
Look for the [OIII]λ4363 line diagnostics for the second AGN candidate.
Examine the stellar mass, metallicity, and SFR estimates for the filament sources.
Review the discussion of direct collapse vs. recoiling BH scenarios for the AGN.

papers.title: Executable verification through formalized expert reasoning in astronomical spectroscopy
papers.authors: Haosong Wang , Ting Tan , Ji Yao , Jiajun Zhang , Qian Zheng , Christophe Yeche , Jean-Paul Kneib , Huanyuan Shan
papers.subjects: Cosmology and Nongalactic Astrophysics (astro-ph.CO) ; Instrumentation and Methods for Astrophysics (astro-ph.IM)
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence has reshaped scientific prediction, but scientific verification remains a human bottleneck. Automated systems can map observations to labels, parameters or hypotheses, yet scientific conclusions require evidence, must satisfy physical consistency, and need explicit testing of alternatives before a decision is made. Here we introduce FORMA (Formalized Observational Reasoning with Auditable Decisions), an executable verification protocol that reconstructs expert reasoning into a workflow: it extracts evidence, generates hypotheses under physical constraints, tests alternatives, and performs auditable consistency checks. Unlike prediction or post-hoc interpretability, executable verification records and tests the evidential path leading to a decision. Astronomical spectroscopy provides a natural testbed, because ambiguous survey spectra are still adjudicated by expert visual inspection. Applied to the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) visual inspection catalogue, FORMA combines template-fitting candidate redshifts, spectral evidence extraction and physical audit into an auditable credibility score. A medium-or-higher credibility threshold identifies $331$ definite predictions with $95.5\%$ binary agreement with expert-adjudicated classes, while increasing credibility is associated with improved redshift consistency and higher classification reliability. These results show that automated inference can be coupled to explicit verification, allowing candidate outputs to be evaluated before they enter scientific use.
papers.Reasons for match: This paper introduces FORMA, an executable verification protocol for astronomical spectroscopy that uses formalized expert reasoning, which is directly relevant to AI/automated classification and spectral inference for astronomy.
papers.Short digest: The central question is how to automate scientific verification in astronomical spectroscopy beyond prediction. The main result is FORMA, which reconstructs expert reasoning into an auditable workflow that achieves 95.5% agreement with experts on DESI data. This matters for my work because it provides a framework for automated, auditable classification of ambiguous spectra, applicable to JWST high-redshift galaxy and AGN surveys.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check the credibility score threshold and its relation to classification reliability.
Look for examples of spectral evidence extraction and physical audit steps.
Examine how the method handles ambiguous cases and compares to expert adjudication.

papers.title: Exploring Image-Text Alignment for Radio Galaxy Morphologies
papers.authors: Erica Lastufka , Mariia Drozdova , Svyatoslav Volosynovskiy
papers.abstract: We investigate whether specially constructed text captions can capture the same morphological information as radio galaxy images. Using the MiraBest dataset, we generate captions with a domain-specific prompt and evaluate their alignment with images through the SigLIP-2 vision--language model, with and without LoRA fine-tuning. Results show that caption-based classification of FR-I and FR-II galaxies performs similarly to images, with fine-tuning improving local coherence of embeddings but not global alignment.
papers.Reasons for match: This paper explores image-text alignment for radio galaxy morphologies using vision-language models, which is directly relevant to AI-for-astronomy and automated classification.
papers.Short digest: The central question is whether text captions can capture the same morphological information as radio galaxy images. The main result is that caption-based classification of FR-I/FR-II galaxies performs similarly to images. This matters for my work because it demonstrates the use of multimodal AI for galaxy classification, which could be extended to JWST data for high-redshift galaxies and AGN.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check the classification performance metrics and comparison between image-only and caption-only models.
Look for details on the domain-specific prompt and LoRA fine-tuning approach.
Examine the dataset (MiraBest) and whether the method could generalize to other morphological classes.

papers.title: Low-Frequency Recombination Lines from Galaxies and AGN over Cosmic Time
papers.authors: Kimberly L. Emig , Sergei Balashev , Francoise Combes , Lucie Cros , Bjorn Emonts , Neeraj Gupta , Antoine Gusdorf , Emmanuel Momjian , Sébastien Muller , Elaine M. Sadler , Pedro Salas , Alexander G. G. M. Tielens , Ilsang Yoon
papers.abstract: Radio recombination lines (RRLs) at low frequencies (<10 GHz) can provide a multi-phase view of interstellar gas in nearby galaxies, absorption-line-systems, and AGN. Hydrogen RRLs arise in fully ionized gas and carbon RRLs trace elusive cold-HI and CO-dark molecular gas. Low frequency RRLs are typically stimulated by the radio continuum and thus may be observable within or against radio bright sources out to cosmological distances (z ~ 6). Although long sought after, RRLs were only recently detected outside of the local universe (z ~ 1; Emig et al., 2020, 2023). Such detections have been made possible by the advancement of wide-bandwidth spectral-line surveys on next-generation low-frequency telescopes. Precursors and pathfinders to the SKA have opened up this field of research and will make significant advancements over the next years by enabling surveys over large source samples. The SKA will provide access to the crucial frequency ranges where RRL line intensity is brightest. Furthermore, multi-band SKA measurements will fully characterize gas physical conditions. Key extragalactic science of low frequency RRLs will focus on (i) the conversion of baryonic material into stars across cosmic time, (ii) the evolution of the ISM and its physical conditions in galaxies, and (iii) how gas drives and inhibits AGN activity.
papers.Reasons for match: This paper discusses low-frequency radio recombination lines from galaxies and AGN over cosmic time, which is relevant to AGN and galaxy evolution, but not directly JWST-based.
papers.Short digest: The central question is how low-frequency RRLs can provide a multi-phase view of interstellar gas in galaxies and AGN out to z~6. The main result is that RRLs trace ionized and molecular gas and are observable with SKA pathfinders. This is partially relevant to my work because it addresses gas and AGN at high redshift, but uses radio rather than JWST observations.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check the detection examples at z~1 and the predicted observability at higher redshift.
Look for discussion of how RRLs distinguish AGN activity from star formation.
Examine the survey strategies and frequency ranges that will be accessible with SKA.

papers.title: Uncertainty-Aware Deep Learning for the Ly$α$ Forest: CNN-Based Absorber Detection and Characterization
papers.authors: Paryag Sharma , Vikram Khaire , Ting-Yun Cheng , Hum Chand , Prakash Gaikwad
papers.abstract: The Ly$\alpha$ forest is a powerful probe of the intergalactic medium and small-scale matter distribution, but deriving absorber properties traditionally requires computationally expensive Voigt-profile fitting. We present a convolutional neural network (CNN) that identifies and characterizes H I Ly$\alpha$ absorbers directly from quasar spectra. The model is trained on synthetic spectra generated from the IllustrisTNG simulation and fitted with the VIPER Voigt-profile fitting code to provide training labels. The network simultaneously predicts absorber presence, column density ($N_{\rm HI}$), Doppler parameter ($b_{\rm HI}$), and line centroid. On simulated spectra, the CNN achieves an F1 score of $\sim$0.8, with mean absolute errors of $\sim$0.18 in $\log N_{\rm HI}$ and $\sim$0.10 in $\log b_{\rm HI}$. It accurately reproduces the H I column density distribution function (CDDF) and the $b_{\rm HI}$--$N_{\rm HI}$ relation, recovering CDDF slopes consistent with VIPER and a lower-envelope relation with an RMS difference of only 0.36 km s$^{-1}$. Applied to high-resolution UVES spectra, performance decreases to an F1 score of $\sim$0.5, with mean absolute errors of $\sim$0.34 in $\log N_{\rm HI}$ and $\sim$0.21 in $\log b_{\rm HI}$. Latent-space analysis reveals a significant domain shift between the simulated and observational spectra, contributing to the reduced performance. Nevertheless, the CNN preserves the observed CDDF and $b_{\rm HI}$--$N_{\rm HI}$ distributions, yielding CDDF slopes consistent with VIPER and a lower-envelope RMS difference of 2.96 km s$^{-1}$. Monte Carlo dropout is implemented during inference to quantify predictive uncertainties. Together with its computational efficiency, the method provides a scalable and uncertainty-aware framework for Ly$\alpha$ forest analysis in upcoming spectroscopic surveys.
papers.Reasons for match: Uses deep learning (CNN) for absorber detection in quasar spectra, relevant to AI-for-astronomy workflows but not directly about high-redshift galaxies or AGN.
papers.Short digest: The paper asks whether a CNN can identify and characterize Lyα absorbers from quasar spectra. It achieves good performance on simulated data but degrades on real UVES spectra. This is relevant as an AI method but not directly applicable to my high-redshift galaxy/AGN focus.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check performance metrics (F1, MAE) on real vs. simulated data.
Look for discussion of domain shift and how it might affect application to JWST spectra.
Examine whether the method could be adapted for emission-line or AGN spectral features.

papers.title: Deep far-UV observations of the ELAIS N1 field using AstroSat: Source catalogue, spectral energy distribution modelling and star formation
papers.authors: Pranjal Chaturrvedi , Akrtiti Sinha , Abhirup Datta , Kanak Saha
papers.abstract: We present a far-ultraviolet (FUV) photometric study of the ELAIS N1 deep field using the Ultra-Violet Imaging Telescope (UVIT) onboard AstroSat, observed in the F154W filter ($\lambda_{\rm eff} = 1541$\,Å) with a total on-source exposure time of 30\,ksec. Level 1 data were reduced using CCDLAB v3.0, yielding source catalogues of 1637 objects at $3\sigma$ and 458 objects at $5\sigma$, with limiting magnitudes of $25.69\,m_{AB}$ and $25.13\,m_{AB}$ respectively. FUV positions are cross-matched against multiwavelength catalogues spanning optical and infrared wavelengths, with redshifts drawn from spectroscopic and photometric sources. Active galactic nuclei (AGN) are identified and excluded via established multiwavelength criteria, leaving a clean sample of star-forming galaxies (SFGs). Spectral energy distribution (SED) modelling is performed using CIGALE, employing a delayed star formation history with an optional late burst, Bruzual \& Charlot stellar population synthesis, Calzetti dust attenuation, and the SKIRTOR AGN module. From the best-fit models, we derive star formation rates (SFRs), total stellar masses, and young stellar masses as a function of redshift. The SFR increases monotonically with redshift, consistent with the evolution of the Star Formation Main Sequence (SFMS). The ratio of young-to-total stellar mass remains approximately constant across $0 < z \lesssim 0.76$, confirming that the sample consists predominantly of secularly evolving systems undergoing steady, self-regulated star formation rather than starburst-driven episodes.
papers.Reasons for match: This paper uses UVIT FUV data and SED fitting with CIGALE to study star-forming galaxies, including AGN exclusion, which is relevant to SED fitting and galaxy evolution, but at low redshift (z<0.76).
papers.Short digest: The central question is how to derive star formation rates and stellar masses from FUV photometry in the ELAIS N1 field. The main result is that the sample consists of secularly evolving systems on the star formation main sequence. This is partially relevant to my work because it demonstrates SED fitting and AGN classification, but at much lower redshift than my focus.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check the AGN exclusion criteria and multiwavelength flags used.
Look at the SED fitting parameters and whether AGN templates were considered.
Examine the derived SFR and stellar mass distributions and their redshift evolution.

papers.title: slicersim: A python package to simulate image slicer spectroscopic observations -- application to the Lazuli Spectrograph
papers.authors: M. Rigault , Y. Copin , G. Aldering , J. Edelstein , G. Furesz , J. Lasker , T. Miller , S. Perlmutter , A. Roy , E. Schlawin , G. Stefansson
papers.subjects: Instrumentation and Methods for Astrophysics (astro-ph.IM) ; Cosmology and Nongalactic Astrophysics (astro-ph.CO)
papers.abstract: Integral Field Spectroscopy (IFS) is a key technique to study galaxies, stellar and planetary systems, and transients, by spatially splitting the scene and dispersing this light onto the detector. This technique is now central for many modern telescopes, including the Lazuli Space Observatory which will host a low spectral-resolution image slicer spectrograph. To prepare for future IFS-equipped instruments and to better understand the systematics of current ones, realistic simulations are needed. We present slicersim, a Python package designed to simulate IFS observations. slicersim is a modular and flexible tool that allows the user to build a scene, define a telescope, a spectrograph, and a detector, and to simulate the resulting observation, including various sources of noise and instrumental effects. The package is designed to be easily extensible to any IFS, with a current focus on that from the Lazuli Space Observatory. In this paper, we present the structure and logic of the package, detailing its main components, and providing an example of its usage. Using slicersim we demonstrate the feasibility of a large cosmology campaign on Lazuli -- a sample of 8000 Type~Ia Supernovae uniformly distributed between $z=0$ and $z=1.5$, observed within the first few years of its operations for a typical average signal-to-noise of 25 per resolution element rest-frame optical wavelengths.
papers.Reasons for match: This paper presents a simulation package for image slicer IFS, which is relevant to JWST NIRSpec IFU or similar instruments, but the application is to supernova cosmology rather than high-redshift galaxies/AGN.
papers.Short digest: The central question is how to simulate image slicer spectroscopic observations for the Lazuli Space Observatory. The main result is the slicersim package that demonstrates feasibility for a large SN Ia cosmology campaign. This is tangentially relevant to my work because IFS simulations could be applied to JWST high-redshift galaxy observations, but the focus is on supernovae.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check the modular structure and whether it can be adapted to JWST NIRSpec IFU simulations.
Look for noise and instrumental effects included in the simulation.
Examine the example usage and whether the package is extensible to other IFS instruments.
